verses.1:
Al-Mizan describes this as a Medinite chapter whose opening verse states its theme: it sets out obligatory rules and then teachings that make believers mindful of them. A sūrah is a collection of statements pursuing one purpose, and the Qur’an uses the term both for the revealed verses sharing that purpose and for the receptacle containing those verses. Apparently derived from sūr al-balad, “the walls of the city,” it denotes what encloses either the verses or their common aim.

Farḍ, unlike ījāb, particularly conveys the decisive cutting of a verdict or law, while ījāb concerns its establishment. With ʿalā, it makes an act incumbent; with lām, it removes a prohibition. Thus, saying that this chapter was revealed and made obligatory means that its laws must be put into practice: commands are practiced by being performed, and prohibitions by being avoided. Its clear communications, in context, include the Verse of Light and what follows it, which explain belief and disbelief, monotheism and polytheism, so as to remind readers of these teachings.

Zinā is unlawful sexual intercourse; intercourse is lawful through marriage, what resembles marriage, or ownership of a female slave (milk al-yamīn). Verse (24:2) explicitly prescribes one hundred lashes as the ḥadd for an adulteress and adulterer. Islamic jurisprudence supplies two exceptions: a married offender is stoned to death (rajm), while a slave receives half the penalty, fifty lashes. The command is addressed to Muslims and implemented by their governing authority, whether the Prophet, an Imam, or an Imam’s representative.

The prohibition of raʾfah—pity—means that the penalty must not be reduced or dismissed through the pity that causes such lenience. “In the matter of Allah’s religion” means in the execution of His law; the condition of belief in Allah and the Last Day emphatically reinforces this prohibition. A ṭāʾifah of believers must witness the punishment so that it becomes a warning against such indecency.

Al-Mizan understands (24:3), despite its declarative form, as an emphatic legal prohibition. Based on narrations from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt, it concerns an adulterer or adulteress whose adultery is publicly known, who has received the legal penalty, and whose repentance is not known: such a person may marry only an adulteress or adulterer, respectively, or a polytheist. It is a decisive verse (muḥkam), neither abrogated nor in need of reinterpretation. Its placement after the penalty indicates that it concerns those punished for adultery, and Qur’anic decorum would not continue to call a repentant person an adulterer or adulteress.

The commentary rejects the view that the verse merely describes the usual inclination of morally corrupted people toward those like themselves, or rebukes adulterers as fit only for adulterers or polytheists while making the final prohibition refer merely to adultery. Both readings conflict with the passage’s context and detach the verse from its concluding clause. It likewise rejects the claim that the later general command to marry the single and fit among slaves abrogates this ruling: the relation is one of a specific rule to a universal one, and a universal statement after a specific one does not abrogate it. It notes that one might argue that the categorical prohibition in (2:221) of marriage with idolaters abrogates the apparent allowance involving a polytheist, and some have consequently proposed a chronology in which (24:3) preceded that prohibition; this remains only a possible claim.

In (24:4), ramy is metaphorical casting of an accusation and is equivalent to qaḍf. The context concerns accusing chaste women (muḥṣanāt) of adultery. An accuser who cannot produce four people who witnessed the act receives eighty lashes, is deemed a transgressor (fāsiq), and has testimony (shahādah) permanently rejected in the Muslim court. Although the wording names chaste women, it is unconditional as to the accuser and includes male and female, free and slave; narrations from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt interpret it this way.

The exception in (24:5) directly modifies the classification of false accusers as transgressors. Yet that classification is the stated basis for refusing their testimony; therefore, when repentance and amendment remove their transgression, they also remove the consequent exclusion of their testimony. Some exegetes restrict the exception to forgiveness of the sin, maintaining permanent rejection of testimony. Al-Mizan holds that an exception after several statements can in itself apply either only to the last statement or to all of them, depending on context. Here it applies directly to the final statement and, because that statement grounds the preceding rule, extends to that rule as well.

For a husband accusing his wife when no other witnesses exist, (24:6-7) requires four successive sworn testimonies that his accusation is true, followed by a fifth calling God’s curse upon him if he lies. The lack of witnesses is natural in such a case: seeking four witnesses would allow the alleged offenders to disperse. In reply, the wife may avert the ḥadd of adultery through four sworn declarations that he lies, followed by a fifth calling God’s curse upon herself if he is truthful. This is liʿān, mutual cursing, and it automatically separates the couple.

Verse (24:10) is a conditional whose main clause is omitted. Its implied sense is that, were it not for Allah’s grace, mercy, return in mercy, and wisdom, people would suffer their opposites. More specifically—and God knows best—without the blessing of religion, mercy toward repentant sinners, and divinely legislated rules ordering human affairs, people would be wretched, destroyed by sins and errors, and deprived of a wisely ordered life.

verses.3:
Al-Mizan holds that (24:3) is an emphatic legal prohibition, though phrased declaratively: an adulterer may marry only an adulteress or polytheist, and an adulteress only an adulterer or polytheist. Based on narrations from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt, this applies where the adultery is publicly known, the offender has received the legal penalty, and repentance is not known. The verse is decisive (muḥkam), not abrogated and not in need of interpretation through another verse. Its placement after the penalty shows that it concerns offenders who have been punished; moreover, Qur’anic courtesy would not label repentant people adulterers or adulteresses.

The commentary rejects two readings: that the verse merely reports the usual attraction of morally corrupted people to their like, and that it merely rebukes adulterers as fit only for adulterers or polytheists while the final prohibition concerns adultery itself. Both conflict with the context and disconnect the verse from its conclusion.

It also rejects the alleged abrogation by the later general command to marry the single and fit among slaves: a universal rule stated after a specific one does not abrogate the specific rule. It notes that one could argue that the categorical prohibition of marriage with idolaters in (2:221) abrogates the apparent allowance involving a polytheist, and some exegetes therefore propose that this verse preceded (2:221). This remains only a possible claim.
verses.4: Al-Mizan explains that ramy, literally throwing or casting, metaphorically means accusing someone of a reprehensible act and is equivalent to qaḍf. Here it concerns accusing chaste women (muḥṣanāt) of adultery. Whoever cannot produce four witnesses who saw the adultery must receive eighty lashes, is classed as a transgressor (fāsiq), and may never have testimony (shahādah) accepted in the Muslim court. Although the verse is unconditional and therefore includes accusers who are male or female, free or slave, this is also the interpretation reported from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan holds that the exception for those who repent and make amends directly concerns the preceding classification of false accusers as transgressors. Since that classification itself grounds the rule that their testimony is never accepted, removing their transgression also removes the exclusion of their testimony. Thus repentance brings both forgiveness and restoration of testimony.

Some exegetes restrict the exception to forgiveness of the sin, leaving testimony permanently inadmissible. The commentary maintains that an exception following several statements can, by itself, apply either only to the last or to all of them; context decides. Here it applies directly to the final statement, but because that statement is the basis for the prior rule, it extends to the prior rule as well.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains that when a husband accuses his wife but has no witnesses other than himself, he must testify four successive times, swearing by Allah that his accusation is true, and then a fifth time invoke God’s curse upon himself if he lies. Such absence of witnesses is natural, since searching for four witnesses would allow the alleged offenders to disperse.
verses.7: Al-Mizan explains that when a husband accuses his wife but has no witnesses other than himself, he must testify four successive times, swearing by Allah that his accusation is true, and then a fifth time invoke God’s curse upon himself if he lies. Such absence of witnesses is natural, since searching for four witnesses would allow the alleged offenders to disperse.
verses.8: Al-Mizan explains that the wife averts the ḥadd for adultery by responding to her husband’s testimonies with four oaths that he lies, followed by a fifth invoking God’s curse upon herself if he is truthful. This procedure is liʿān, mutual cursing in Islamic law, and automatically separates the couple.
verses.9: Al-Mizan explains that the wife averts the ḥadd for adultery by responding to her husband’s testimonies with four oaths that he lies, followed by a fifth invoking God’s curse upon herself if he is truthful. This procedure is liʿān, mutual cursing in Islamic law, and automatically separates the couple.
verses.10: Al-Mizan explains that the verse is a conditional with its main clause omitted: without Allah’s grace, mercy, return in mercy, and wisdom, people would suffer their opposites. More specifically—and God knows best—without religion, mercy toward repentant sinners, and divinely legislated rules that order life, people would be wretched, destroyed by sins and errors, and deprived of a wisely ordered life.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan explains if as an unqualified lie: something diverted from its proper form, whether belief, action, or speech. ʿUṣbah is a united, mutually supporting group. The verse addresses the believers generally, including believers, hypocrites, and those with sickness in their hearts; it does not address only the Prophet, the accused parties, or merely those distressed by the affair, since such readings disrupt the sustained general address and lack warrant in the wording.

The definite al-if denotes a particular lie. The perpetrators were a coordinated band conspiring to circulate it, tarnish the Prophet’s household, and discredit him. Thus, “a band” is the predicate’s emphasis, not “from among you”; the contrary reading, which makes the verse chiefly a consolation to the Prophet and those upset by the slander, does not fit the verses’ theme.

The event was good for the believing community because a sound society must identify those pursuing deviation and mischief, so it can correct itself. In a community joined to revelation, such an event also brings divine admonition concerning what it has neglected, making people more cautious in religion. Each slanderer bears the evil consequence of his sin, which marks and exposes them, discrediting those who intended to discredit the Prophet. The alternative that the good belongs only to the victims as a reward for their suffering depends on the implausible restricted addressee.

Kibrahu refers to the main or greater part of the slander. The one who assumed that principal role and persisted in spreading it will receive a grievous chastisement.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan says that the verse rebukes believing men and women for neither dismissing the report nor thinking well of the accused believers. “Their own people” means themselves, rather than merely using a pronoun, to show that faith should restrain a person from evil and indecency in speech and action. Believers share the garment and implications of faith as though they were one soul; therefore, each must think well of another and not describe another by what he does not know.

They should have declared the report an evident falsehood. Any report one does not know, or claim made without supporting evidence, is legally treated as a lie whether or not it happens to be true in fact, as indicated by: But as they have not brought witnesses they are liars before Allah (24:13).
verses.13: Al-Mizan holds that a truthful accusation of adultery requires four witnesses. Without them, the claim is legally ruled false and its makers are liars in the shariah.
verses.14: Al-Mizan explains ifāḍah in speech as plunging or immersing oneself in it. Linked to the rebuke in (24:12), the verse warns believers that, but for Allah’s grace and mercy in this world and the hereafter, grievous chastisement would have afflicted them in both realms for plunging into the slander.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains talaqqī of speech as receiving it from another. Receiving the slander “with your tongues” depicts its unexamined passage from one speaker to another; speaking “with your mouths” further shows speech that never reached the heart’s investigation or assurance.

The believers plunged into the slander by transmitting what they did not know. They treated this as a minor matter, although it was grievous before Allah as a false allegation and slander; because it concerned the Prophet, its circulation also discredited him and impaired his religious call.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan treats this as a further rebuke, linked to the command in (24:12) concerning the believers’ response upon hearing the slander. They should have said that they had no right to utter it and glorified God. The Qur’an’s declaration of an accused person’s innocence is accompanied by God’s glorification, affirming His freedom from defects.

Buhtān means iftirāʾ, a false accusation or slander, and is so called because it stuns and confounds its victim. It was a great buhtān both because it concerned dignity and reputation, particularly the Prophet’s, and because it was made without knowledge or evidence.
verses.17: Al-Mizan says that Allah admonishes believers never to repeat this sin if they are believers, while making His communications clear as the Knowing, Wise One.
verses.18: Al-Mizan says that Allah admonishes believers never to repeat this sin if they are believers, while making His communications clear as the Knowing, Wise One.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan considers the verse apparently revealed with the preceding slander verses. Its reference to al-fāḥishah justifies the threat against unsupported accusations of adultery: since adultery is indecency, desiring its report to circulate among believers is desiring indecency’s circulation.

Yet al-fāḥishah is unrestricted and embraces every indecency, including zinā, qaḍf, and the dissemination of slanderous reports. Those who love such circulation face grievous chastisement in this world and the hereafter. “Chastisement in this world” should not be restricted to the legal penalty (ḥadd), for that interpretation improperly limits both al-fāḥishah to slanderous accusation and circulation to this particular tongue-to-tongue report. Moreover, an accusation itself incurs the legal penalty without depending on its dissemination; if the worldly chastisement meant that penalty, the qualification concerning circulation would be unnecessary. “Allah knows, while you do not know” intensifies His wrath and displeasure at an act whose gravity people do not recognize.
verses.20: Al-Mizan says that the verse repeats Allah’s favor and mercy toward the believers, affirming that He is Gentle and Compassionate.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains that the repeated reference to Allah’s grace and mercy is a further favor to the believers and confirms that the slander concerned the Prophet, whose honor and standing explain this emphasis. Here the conditional “were it not” explicitly gives its result: without Allah’s grace and mercy, none would ever have been pure. This accords with the rational and Qur’anic principle that all good and success come from God.

Allah purifies whom He wills, but His will to purify is directed to those who prepare themselves for it. Such preparedness is equivalent to requesting purification through the lisān al-istiʿdād. Allah is Hearing because He hears the request of one who seeks purification, and Knowing because He knows the state of one prepared for it.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan notes that ītilāʾ can mean failing or defaulting, ceasing or abandoning, or swearing and vowing. Accordingly, those possessing grace and abundance should neither fail to give, cease giving, nor swear to withhold support from relatives, the poor, and those who have fled in Allah’s way.

Instead, the wealthy should pardon them and overlook their faults. Allah urges this forgiveness by asking whether they do not love His forgiveness and by declaring Himself Forgiving and Merciful. If the verse is connected with the preceding slander verses, it indicates that some believers had resolved to stop charitable support for people involved in the scandal; God forbids this and directs them to continue their giving.
verses.23: Al-Mizan explains iḥṣān here as ʿiffah: chastity, temperance, and self-restraint. The accused women’s chastity, belief, and unawareness of evil each independently make their accusation wrong, the accuser a wrongdoer, and the accused a victim of wrongdoing. Their combination makes the offense still graver, deserving curse and grievous chastisement in this world and the hereafter. Although revealed in the particular setting of the slander, the verse is general.
verses.24: Al-Mizan takes “the day” as the time of the grievous chastisement mentioned in (24:23). Since “what they did” is unrestricted, the testimony of tongues, hands, and feet concerns all evil deeds, not merely the accusation at issue. Each organ testifies to sins proper to it: the tongue to slander, lying, and backbiting, and the limbs to acts such as carrying gossip and slander between people. Hands and feet are specifically named because most bodily sins are committed through them.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan first reads dīn in its contextual sense of jazāʾ, retribution or recompense, and tawfiyah as full payment: on the Day of Resurrection Allah will pay them their due recompense in full, and they will know that He is the evident Truth.

Read independently, however, dīn may mean one’s path, approach, and way of life. This yields the more sublime sense that realities will appear to humanity on that Day, and better accords with the statement that they will know Allah as the evident Truth. Allah is Truth without any veil and the most evident of all realities; He cannot be unknown through jahl, though creatures may be heedless of Him despite His ultimate evidentness. Thus, knowing God means the removal of heedlessness of Him, and this is what becomes clear on the Day of Resurrection, as in: Certainly you were heedless of it, but now We have removed from you your veil, so your sight today is sharp (50:22).
verses.26:
Al-Mizan says that the verse concludes the slander account but has universal content. Its closing declaration that “they are clear of what they say” shows that al-khabīthāt, al-khabīthīn, al-ṭayyibāt, and al-ṭayyibīn denote women and men characterized by vileness or goodness.

Goodness is constituted by belief and chastity. Chaste believing men and women belong to one another and are legally clear of accusations unsupported by evidence. By their faith they qualify for forgiveness and a noble provision: a good life in this world and good reward in the hereafter.

Vile women and men are unbelievers, whose khubth is an inner impurity that has deprived them of faith; they are assigned to one another because they are alike. They are not clear of indecency, but the verse does not assert that every unbeliever actually commits it. The verse therefore describes all believing men and women as good, despite its particular occasion, and grants these blessings according to their outward status: God honors them for faith, while unbelievers stand in the opposite position.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains istīnās as seeking a peaceful, familiar relation before entering another’s house. It is practically done by mentioning God’s name or making a sound such as tanaḥnuḥ, thereby informing the owner of one’s presence and wish to enter, so that he may prepare if he is in a state he does not wish others to see.

Seeking permission before entry, followed by salutation, protects people’s private affairs and the believers’ honor, and reassures the owner that the entrant bears no ill will. Persistent observance strengthens brotherhood, friendship, and mutual support in revealing what is fair and concealing what is foul; this is the social happiness meant by “this is better for you, that you may be mindful.” An interpretation that the phrase calls people to heed God’s admonitions and understand their reasons is acceptable. The claim that the order should be reversed, so that salutation precedes permission, is plainly implausible.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan explains that if one knows no person is present to grant permission, one must not enter another’s house, since the owner’s permission has not been obtained. The verse does not authorize peeking inside to determine whether anyone is there; these rules are directed against looking into and discovering people’s private affairs.

Its first part governs entry where nobody is available to permit it, while its second governs the case where permission is refused: if told to go back, one must go back. This is purer, and Allah knows what people do.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan takes “houses” to have two qualifications: they are uninhabited and are places wherein one has matāʿ, apparently meaning istimtāʿ—enjoyment, usufruct, or utility—rather than a particular commodity. Though it is less likely, the latter phrase may instead explain why entry entails no sin.

The verse therefore permits entry without permission into non-residential places established for public needs, such as rest areas, bathhouses, and mills; their purpose indicates a universal permission to enter. Some exegetes interpret matāʿ as merchandise and limit the ruling to places such as markets and shops where one has goods, but Al-Mizan judges this only remotely compatible with the wording.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan explains ghaḍḍ as closing the eyelids and abṣār as eyes. The particle min indicates the point from which looks are cast down and curtailed; it is neither superfluous, generic, nor partitive. Since the clause is presented as the complement of the imperative “say,” it conveys a command: believers are ordered to cast down their eyes, or prohibited from looking at what is unlawful to see among unrelated men and women.

Furūj, a courteous Qur’anic expression for private organs, are likewise to be guarded. Although some interpret this as guarding against adultery and sodomy, its conjunction with casting down the eyes indicates guarding one’s private parts from others’ looks. A narration from al-Ṣādiq states that, unlike other Qur’anic verses concerning guarding private parts, this verse prohibits unlawful looking. On that basis, the verse prohibits looking at others’ private parts and commands covering one’s own. The ruling is described as purer for believers, while Allah is Aware of what they do.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan holds that believing women, like believing men, must turn their eyes from unlawful sights and cover their private parts from unrelated men and women. “Displaying ornaments” means displaying the bodily places on which ornaments are worn, not the ornaments themselves. The exception for what ordinarily appears is, according to narrations, the face, hands, and feet.

Khumur are head-coverings, and women are commanded to let their ends fall over the juyūb, here meaning the chest or bosom. Ornaments may be displayed to husbands and to the specified close male relatives by blood or marriage; grandfathers of husbands and grandsons of husbands share the rule of fathers-in-law and husbands’ sons. “Their women” denotes Muslim women, so Muslim women may not uncover before non-Muslim women. “Those whom their right hands possess” includes both male and female servants.

Dependent men without sexual need are, as narrated, mentally disabled persons under others’ guardianship who have no sexual desire. The children excepted are all children not yet capable of the concealed affairs of women, an expression referring to puberty. Women must also not strike their feet so as to make hidden ornaments audible. Finally, the command to turn to Allah means repenting through obedience to His commands and abstention from His prohibitions—following His path—in hope of success.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan explains al-inkāḥ as giving in marriage, al-ayāmā as unmarried men and women, and al-ṣāliḥīn here as those fit for marriage rather than those righteous in conduct. The verse thus commands that single people and marriageable male and female slaves be married.

Its promise that the needy will be made free from want is a promise of wealth and abundance, reinforced by Allah’s being Ample-giving and Knowing. Every being receives rizq according to its capacity to receive, by God’s mashiyyah.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan explains that those unable to afford a wife’s dowry and expenses must practice istiʿfāf, that is, abstinence and chastity, guarding themselves from adultery until Allah grants them financial sufficiency.

Al-kitāb means mukātabah: a contract under which a slave is freed in return for payment earned through labor. Masters are ordered to grant it when they know good in the slave, meaning that the slave is fit and suitable for freedom. Giving them from God’s wealth refers either to the legal allocation of obligatory zakāh toward their contracted manumission, as in and the (ransoming of) captives (9:60), or to moral advice that owners reduce the agreed payment.

The verse also forbids compelling slave women or girls into prostitution for the transient wealth of worldly life when they wish to remain chaste; taḥassun may mean chastity or marriage. This condition is stated because compulsion does not arise where they lack the desire for chastity. If they are compelled, Allah promises them forgiveness and mercy after their compulsion.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan explains mathal as ṣifah, or description. The verse may independently declare that God has sent clarifying communications containing the religious teachings by which salvation is attained; descriptions of prior people, both righteous and wicked, so that people may discern what to adopt and abandon; and an admonition for the God-conscious.

Alternatively, the initial “and” may mean “while,” making the verse a description of those addressed in the preceding command to turn to Allah.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan begins with the defining feature of nūr: light is manifest in itself and makes otherwise dark objects manifest. The term can therefore extend from visible light to every sense that discloses its object, then to intellect insofar as it manifests intelligible realities. Existence itself is the fullest instance of manifestation, because a thing becomes manifest to itself and others by existing. Contingent beings possess existence only through God’s act of bringing them into being, so their light is borrowed. God is the independent light who gives existence and manifestation to everything, which is why He is called the light of the heavens and the earth. This does not reduce Him to a physical or borrowed luminosity; it means that He is the source by whom all things appear and subsist.

Because everything’s manifestation occurs through God, no being is wholly ignorant of Him. Before a thing can apprehend its own manifestation, God’s intrinsic manifestation is already making that apprehension possible. The universal light in the verse is therefore equivalent to the existence and appearance bestowed upon every being—an expression of universal divine mercy.

“The likeness of His light,” however, turns to a special manifestation. The light now belongs to God as something He shines upon others, and the closing statement that He guides to it whom He wills shows that it is not simply the universal existence shared by all. It is the light of faith and maʿrifah bestowed upon true believers, illuminating their path toward Him. Al-Mizan rejects identifying it narrowly with the Qur’an, since believers before its revelation also possessed this light and the Qur’an describes it as a quality borne by believers. The Qur’an can be called their light only insofar as it unveils truth for them, which returns to the same meaning of faith and gnosis.

The comparison embraces the whole image rather than the niche alone. A niche concentrates and directs illumination; within it a lamp provides the light, while its glass steadies and intensifies the flame until it resembles a brilliant star. The lamp is fueled by pure oil from a blessed olive tree that is neither eastern nor western. This does not mean an otherworldly tree or one placed geographically between East and West. It describes a tree exposed to sunlight throughout the day rather than shaded for half of it, so its fruit ripens fully and yields exceptionally pure oil, almost luminous even before fire touches it.

“Light upon light” may express limitless intensity rather than two independently existing lights. It can also indicate two ascriptions of one light: the lamp possesses the light primarily, while the glass appears luminous by receiving and transmitting it. On that reading, the image precisely fits faith and gnosis in believers. Their light is real in them but borrowed from God, dependent upon and drawn from His light. The niche focuses it, the glass stabilizes and magnifies it, and the perfectly receptive oil displays its readiness to shine. Together the elements depict divine guidance concentrated in believing hearts with the highest clarity, strength, and excellence.

God’s guiding “whom He will” explains why believers benefit from this special light while disbelievers do not. The divine will is not portrayed as arbitrary preference detached from the recipients’ qualities. The later description of people whom commerce does not distract from remembrance identifies those willed for this guidance as persons perfected in faith. Their character and conduct give them the capacity to receive the light, whereas chosen disbelief makes others unreceptive.

The conclusion that God sets forth parables and knows all things signals that the image contains deep realities not exhausted by its surface. A parable makes transcendent knowledge accessible to learned and unlearned hearers alike, while each receives from it according to capacity. The imagery thus unites God’s universal manifestation of all existence with His special illumination of receptive hearts without confusing the independent source of light with the borrowed light of creatures.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan explains that idhn is permission, while the raising of these houses means elevation in rank, honor, and esteem. Since all honor belongs to God, any honor granted to another derives from its relation to Him. These houses are elevated because God’s name is remembered in them continually, or because they permanently possess the capacity for such remembrance. Mosques are an example, being established for the remembrance of God.

The connection with the preceding verse may be read either as continuing the image of the niche or as continuing the statement that God guides whom He wills to His light; either reading gives the same result. Their glorification in mornings and evenings means continual glorification, not worship confined to those two times. Tasbīḥ is to believe and declare that God is free from whatever does not befit His sanctity.

The commentary notes that the verse mentions tasbīḥ rather than taḥmīd because declaring God free from defect is preliminary to pure maʿrifah. Once limitations and defects have been negated from Him, His perfection is realized and He may be praised. Taḥmīd proclaims His perfections and accompanies the realization of His light of maʿrifah, whereas tasbīḥ declares His transcendence from all unbefitting qualities. The verse therefore mentions the preliminary quality that prepares believers for guidance to God’s light.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains that tijārah denotes a continuing occupation of buying and selling, whereas bayʿ denotes an individual sale. By separately negating both, the verse shows that these men are distracted neither continually by their occupation nor occasionally by a particular transaction. An acceptable further explanation is that the profit expected from a particular sale is more immediate and certain than the speculative gain of trade as an occupation; freedom from the latter does not necessarily entail freedom from the former.

Prayer and poor-rate stand for all obligatory good deeds: prayer represents duties owed to God, and poor-rate duties owed to people. Since these acts are themselves forms of remembrance, the separate mention of the remembrance of Allah signifies abiding attentiveness and presence of heart. Thus, nothing distracts them either from their permanent inward remembrance or from their intermittent practical remembrance through prayer, almsgiving, and the other obligations.

The day when hearts and eyes turn about is the Day of Resurrection, and encompasses believers and disbelievers alike. Its turning results from the unveiling of realities: souls and their insights are turned away from worldly perceptions that veiled them from God and truth, toward another vision through the light of īmān and maʿrifah. Believers who possess this light behold God’s magnanimity and munificence, while disbelievers remain blind and encounter what distresses them.

The verse singles out hearts and eyes because faith and divine knowledge are precisely what illuminate them on that day. The believers fear this overturning because it may result in deprivation from God’s light and from witnessing His bounty, which is eternal damnation and punishment. In this respect, their fear is of the evil within themselves.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan takes the opening “that” to state the purpose of the believers’ righteous deeds. God rewards every prescribed good deed, but giving them the “best reward” means that He treats each deed according to the best deed of its kind. He mends and purifies their acts rather than scrutinizing imperfections that would diminish their worth; hence they are not subjected to meticulous reckoning.

His granting them more from His faḍl means a bestowal beyond the recompense corresponding to their deeds. Since the believers are promised whatever they wish, this “more” is something beyond even the highest human wish. It is an exceptional Qur’anic promise to believers.

“Allah gives sustenance to whom He will without reckoning” independently grounds both promises in God’s will. Rizq is a bestowal wholly from Him: creatures neither determine its distribution nor possess an entitlement against Him. Believers qualify through their deeds for a fitting reward, yet God grants them, without close accounting, the value of their best deeds and then an additional gift surpassing what they can desire.

Although no one possesses an original entitlement to God’s rizq, God has promised sustenance and thereby grants an entitlement to basic provision according to people’s work and effort. No entitlement exists to what exceeds this; additional blessings have no cause but His will.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan explains that the disbelievers’ deeds are like a sarāb, a desert mirage that appears to be water but has no reality. The analogy concerns acts of worship, offerings, and litanies by which they seek nearness to their gods. The verse mentions the thirsty person because he is driven by thirst to pursue the apparent water, only to find nothing when he arrives.

Disbelievers, like all people, seek felicity in accordance with their fiṭrah and strive for it through their actions. Yet neither their deeds nor the gods from whom they expect reward can bring them to that goal. The wording that he “comes to it” suggests that God awaits him: instead of finding the hoped-for water or the efficacy of his gods, he finds God, Who encompasses his deeds and fully repays his reckoning. This is likened to their return to God at death, when the time for action ends. Having turned from remembrance and righteous deeds that lead to God’s light, they exhaust their lives in empty acts; in the next abode they find neither the expected return nor any authority in their gods.

God is quick in reckoning because His knowledge encompasses all things equally, whether great or small, subtle or conspicuous, old or new. Though the verse primarily concerns rejecters of divine religion, especially polytheists and idolaters, it also applies to atheists. Those who deny the Creator direct their actions toward supposed powers such as nature, matter, or time and seek happiness only in worldly life. At death, they discover that their hopes were imaginary and their deeds yielded nothing, and God fully repays their reckoning.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan presents this as the second analogy for the disbelievers’ deeds. Their deeds are dense veils over their hearts, preventing the light of maʿrifah. They are like darkness in a turbulent deep sea: a wave covers it, another wave lies above that, and a cloud above both blocks the light of sun, moon, and stars. These are compounded layers of darkness, so intense that a person can scarcely see his own outstretched hand, the nearest and most readily visible part of himself.

Disbelievers are travelling toward God through their actions, but are like one crossing such a sea with no light by which to see or find the shore of deliverance. They have no light because God has not given it to them. Since He is the Light of everything and the sole giver of light, whatever He does not assign light possesses none.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan argues that all beings in the heavens and earth are contingent rather than self-existent or independent; their existence comes from God, the final terminus of all need. Every being displays both its own existence and the existence of the One who bestows existence on it. In this sense, each is illuminated by God and proves the Light that manifests it. Its very being glorifies God by negating independence from every other thing and denying the lordship of anything besides Him; it points to One free of need, limitation, and imperfection. Thus the verse proves that God is the Light of the heavens and the earth through the appearance of the things He brings into existence.

The verse explicitly names intelligent beings in the heavens and earth and birds in flight, although all things glorify God. Perhaps these are singled out as particularly marvelous signs of creation. An alternative interpretation makes “everyone in the heavens and the earth” include all beings and treats their glorification as lisān al-ḥāl, a proof so forceful that it resembles spoken speech. The commentary rejects this alternative because the verse ascribes knowledge of prayer and glorification to them.

“Do you not see” indicates that this glorification is certain and evident, since certain knowledge is commonly called seeing. The address may be general to all intelligent beings, or particularly to the Prophet as one to whom hidden dimensions of the heavens and earth were unveiled. The verse genuinely ascribes to the beings knowledge of their prayer and glorification. Al-Mizan rejects both the view that God is the subject of “knows,” since the verse then separately says that Allah knows what they do, and the view that their knowledge is merely metaphorical.

The verse mentions tasbīḥ rather than taḥmīd because its concern is tawḥīd and the refutation of polytheism. Tasbīḥ negates limitation and imperfection from the true God, whereas prayer here means duʿāʾ, expressing the supplicant’s need and God’s freedom from need. This too accords more directly with tasbīḥ.

Because the verse ascribes glorification and knowledge to all, believers and disbelievers alike, it establishes a universal light shared by all beings, alongside the particular light reserved for God’s friends among believers. These correspond to His universal and particular mercy; the latter is the light described as “light upon light.” Finally, God’s knowledge of what creatures do includes their glorification, even where it occurs through their mere existence. For believers this is acknowledgment and encouragement that He knows and will reward their glorification; for disbelievers it completes the proof against them, since His knowledge includes the records of their existential glorification and their voluntary denial.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan reads this verse as joining the preceding proof of God’s universal light with the following proof that He grants His particular light exclusively. God’s sole kingdom and sovereignty over the heavens and earth establish both the comprehensiveness of His universal light and His complete authority to give His particular light to whomever He wills. He does what He wills and rules as He wills.

By restricting all sovereignty to God, the verse implies that no other king exists and that all things return to Him. “To Allah is the eventual coming” therefore concerns God as the reference point and return of all affairs, not merely their return in the hereafter. God knows best.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan explains the verse as an address to every person capable of receiving its evidence. God drives dispersed clouds, gathers them, and piles them one upon another, so that rain emerges through their openings and falls upon the earth. He also sends down abundant, concentrated hail, likened to mountains, afflicting whomever He wills and turning it away from whomever He wills; the brightness of its lightning nearly blinds the sight.

In context, this illustrates why the special divine light belongs only to those to whom God gives it. The giving of light is wholly His affair, just as He sends beneficial rain when He wills and sends hail that strikes some and spares others when He wills.
verses.44: Al-Mizan explains that God’s turning over of night and day means His exchanging and replacing one with the other. It is another sign that the affairs of the world return to God’s will alone, and a lesson for those who have sight.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan takes the diversity of living creatures, despite their common creation from water, as another illustration that all affairs return to God’s will. The verse mentions creatures that move on their bellies, on two feet, and on four feet only as sufficient representative categories. Their differing forms show that God creates what He wills; He may bestow universal light and mercy upon all creatures and particular light and mercy upon some alone.

“Surely Allah has power over all things” explains why His creative will is unrestricted: His power is absolute and unconditional. If the occurrence of an act depended on anything beyond His will, His power would itself be conditional and therefore not absolute.

The commentary considers an apparent problem. Contingent things ultimately proceed from the Necessary Being, yet many material things depend on intermediate causes, conditions, and preparations. Considered separately, an individual seems to require, besides God, such conditions as parents, time, and place. These would be parts of its complete cause, so that God would be the complete cause only of the universe as a whole and of the first emanation (al-ṣādir al-awwal), not of every individual contingent thing.

Al-Mizan proposes a subtler view: every contingent being’s causal connections are internal to its own concrete reality and identity. Zayd, for example, is not an isolated individual to which parents, time, place, prior events, and accompanying events are subsequently added; his reality includes all the contingent beings and events to which his existence is tied. Taken in this complete reality, he depends only on the Necessary Being. God is therefore his complete cause, and his existence requires only God’s will, not any extraneous cause, condition, or preparation. This is the sense in which God’s power over every being is absolute and unconditional.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains that the clear communications are the Verse of Light and the verses following it that describe God’s light. The straight path is the way whose travellers are safe from error and God’s wrath.

The verse says simply that clear communications have been revealed, rather than that they were revealed “to you.” This wording distinguishes revelation, which verbally explains and identifies the path, from the guidance by which Allah brings whomever He wills to the straight path. Had the verse said that these communications were revealed to its audience, the following statement about guidance might suggest that everyone who reads them is thereby guided. That is not so, since some readers are hypocrites or have disease in their hearts. God knows best.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse concerns hypocrites who profess belief and obedience, then abandon what their profession entails. Belief in God is acceptance of His unity and revealed religion, and obedience to Him is acting by what He has legislated. Belief in the Messenger is acceptance that he is sent by God, that his commands, prohibitions, and judgments are God’s rather than his own; obeying him means complying with his commands, prohibitions, rulings, and judgments.

Belief in and obedience to God concern commitment to the religion itself, while belief in and obedience to the Messenger concern his truthful communication of that religion and his decisions in disputes. The verse’s separate wording for God and the Messenger indicates this difference in scope, though the two beliefs cannot be separated. Thus the claim means that its speakers have committed themselves to God’s religion and to the Messenger’s truthfulness and just judgment. When some then turn back, they violate the implications of their own claim. Al-Mizan holds that “these are not believers” rebukes all who make this claim, not merely the subgroup explicitly said to turn back.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan takes the tone of the verse to suggest its revelation concerning a hypocrite who, after a dispute, refused to submit the case to the Prophet’s judgment. The Prophet judges only by God’s rule and revelation; his judgments are therefore attributable directly to him and, through God’s law and appointment of him to judge, to God.

To be called to God is to be directed to what God’s religion requires in the dispute, while to be called to the Messenger is to follow the Prophet’s direct ruling. The pronoun in “that he may judge between them” apparently refers to the Messenger; its singular form shows that his judgment is identical with God’s judgment. This verse presents a particular instance of the general turning-away described in the preceding verse.
verses.49: Al-Mizan explains idhʿān as inqiyād, obedience or compliance. The wording that they “come to him” shows that “the truth” means the Messenger’s judgment, which is inseparable from truth because he judges by it. They readily and obediently seek his ruling only when it favors them; their refusal when it is against them shows that they follow desire rather than truth.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan interprets the disease in their hearts as weakness of faith, not hypocrisy, since their lack of true belief has already been stated. Irt iyāb means shakk, and, being unrestricted, includes any religious doubt arising after belief, not merely doubt about the Prophet’s competence or justice as judge. Ḥayf means injustice or wrong.

Their avoidance of the Prophet’s judgment might seem to arise from weak faith, religious doubt, or fear that God’s law would not give each party its due, or that the Prophet would fail to observe truth and rights. But there is no possibility of injustice in the judgment of God and His Messenger. Al-Mizan reads bal, “Nay,” as replacing all three possibilities: if weakness or doubt were the cause, they would not submit even when judgment favored them. Their actual cause is therefore their own injustice.

This injustice apparently means hypocrisy: they verbally acknowledge īmān while practically violating its conditions and implications. It may more specifically mean injustice concerning nonfinancial rights, but not injustice in an unrestricted sense, since that would include the preceding alternatives rather than replace them. A translator’s note qualifies Al-Mizan’s reading of bal: it argues that the replacement is certainly directed to the final possibility alone, so that “they themselves are the unjust” may retain its unrestricted sense and include disease of heart and religious doubt.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan regards this verse as stating an inseparable practical consequence of īmān. Belief in God and His Messenger commits the heart to their decree, and its continuing expression—indicated by kāna—is that, when believers are called to their judgment, they say, “We hear and we obey.” They do not reject such a call, for rejection lies outside the bounds of belief; success belongs exclusively to those who respond in this way.

The invitation apparently means that one party in a dispute asks the other to refer the matter to God and the Messenger, as indicated by idhā, “when,” which denotes a particular occurrence rather than the enduring divine command to refer disputes to their judgment. Al-Mizan rejects the view that God and the Messenger themselves are the grammatical subject of the invitation, though every such call ultimately derives from them. It allows that the divine call may also mean the command to refer disputes to their rule; interpreting it as submission to the ruling itself is unlikely because the wording speaks of an invitation.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan explains fawz as felicity or success, akin to falāḥ. The verse supplies the general rationale for the preceding declaration that believers who answer the call to God’s and the Messenger’s judgment are successful: genuine acceptance of that judgment entails obedience to God and His Messenger, inward fear of God, and outward consciousness of duty to Him; whoever possesses these qualities is felicitous.

The promise applies to both parties in a dispute: those who summon others to God’s and the Messenger’s ruling and those who accept that summons.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan explains jahda aymānihim as their strongest and most strenuous oaths. “Going forth” apparently means leaving for jihad. They swear emphatically that they will go if commanded, but are told not to swear: going forth is already a known obligation of obedience, and God knows their deeds and is not deceived by the force of their vows. Ṭāʿah maʿrūfah is therefore understood as a predicate with an omitted subject: going forth is known obedience.

Other exegetes interpret “going forth” as surrendering homes and possessions if the Messenger judges against them, and ṭāʿah maʿrūfah as honorable obedience, better than oaths. Although this fits the preceding context more closely, Al-Mizan rejects it because the people in question have already turned away when summoned to the Prophet’s judgment. It would make no sense for them to swear that they would submit property if he ruled so. If the oath-makers were different people, there would be no evidence for giving “going forth” that particular meaning.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan says that the verse commands obedience to God in His revealed religion and obedience to the Messenger both in what he conveys from God and in all his religious and worldly commands. The opening “Say” shows that obedience is wholly due to God; obedience to the Messenger is obedience to his Sender precisely because he is a messenger.

If people turn away, they do not harm the Messenger: he is responsible only for his assigned task, and they for theirs. Yet obeying him brings guidance, because his message and commands are from God, so obeying him is obeying God. His sole duty is clear delivery of the message; this both absolves him of blame for their deviation and establishes why obedience to him is obedience to God.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan considers the verse apparently Medinan and a promise, to the believers who do righteous deeds among the Muslims, of a righteous society: God will grant them succession in the land, firmly establish their approved religion, exchange fear for security, and enable them to worship Him without associating anything with Him. The address initially includes all Muslims, including hypocrites and wrongdoers, but min in minkum is partitive: the promise belongs only to those among them who believe and do good.

Istikhlāf is more likely the inheritance and governance of the land by one people after another than divine khilāfah. Thus “those before them” are the believing survivors among earlier prophetic nations, not the prophets themselves. Qur’anic usage does not call earlier prophets “those before them,” and the Israelites are also an unsuitable comparison: their society after Pharaoh was mixed with disbelief, hypocrisy, and wrongdoing, whereas the promised society consists of believers who do righteous deeds. If the comparison concerned succession alone, there would be no reason to restrict it to Israel rather than other powerful nations. The promised succession depends on the collective righteousness of the society, not on the righteousness of a specified individual.

Tamkīn means the religion’s secure and effective stability: its fundamental teachings are neither disputed nor denied, and its laws are not neglected. The approved religion is islām, called “their religion” both in honor of them and because it accords with fiṭrah. The exchange of fear for security covers the believers’ hardships under disbelievers and hypocrites and means security from every internal and external, open and hidden enemy, in religious and worldly affairs. “They shall serve Me, not associating aught with Me” describes their condition in this security and negates every apparent and hidden form of shirk; God alone is worshiped throughout the society, and no distinction or advantage remains except taqwā. Kafara after this promise apparently means kufrān, ingratitude rather than disbelief: one who responds to the fulfilled favor through denial, hypocrisy, or grievous sin is fully transgressive, for fisq is departure from the bounds of servitude.

Al-Mizan reports views that the verse was fulfilled in the Companions through the Rightly-Guided Caliphs, or in the whole Muslim ummah through Islam’s post-Prophetic expansion. It also reports the view that it concerns the promised Mahdi, with “those who believe and do good” identified as the Prophet and the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt. It rejects identifying the promised group, on the verse’s wording or reason alone, with the Companions, the Prophet, the Imams, or the entire ummah. Such identifications impose more than the text states.

The commentary’s conclusion is that the verse promises a society free of disbelief, hypocrisy, and evildoing, governed in belief and practice solely by the true religion, and secure from all enemies, oppression, and tyranny. No such society has existed since the Prophet’s time. It therefore properly corresponds only to the society formed after the appearance of the Mahdi, as described in mutawātir narrations from the Prophet and the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt; the verse concerns that righteous society, not the Mahdi alone.

This does not make the promise irrelevant to those alive at revelation. The address is to persons as bearers of the stated qualities, not merely as particular individuals, and therefore extends to all who possess them, even if the original audience does not witness its fulfillment. A looser, nonliteral reading could instead treat the promise as Islam’s outward dominance, formal religious identity, and visible rituals throughout the wider ummah, despite division and lack of inward security or truth. Even on that reading, it cannot be confined to the Four Rightly-Guided Caliphs, the first three of them, or ʿAlī alone.
verses.56:
Al-Mizan explains that maintaining prayer and paying the poor-rate command obedience to God’s legislation. They are singled out as major pillars of duty: prayer represents duty to God and the poor-rate duty to people. Obedience to the Messenger concerns his judicial and governmental authority.

The promise of mercy supplies the reason for these commands: through obedience to God and the Messenger, it is hoped that divine mercy will cover them and that God will fulfill, or hasten, His promise. If hypocrisy disappears, Muslims become righteous, and they unite in supporting the truth, this will help bring about the righteous society that contains every good.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan says that this verse confirms the preceding promise of succession, established religion, and security. God emphatically reassures the Prophet that disbelievers cannot frustrate Him or prevent His promise through their power. It is glad tidings to him of God’s favor to his community and of his enemies’ defeat.

Although phrased as a prohibition against thinking that disbelievers can escape, it functions as a declaration that they will be defeated in this world and that the Fire will be their evil abode in the hereafter.
verses.58:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse qualifies the general command to seek permission before entering homes: servants and prepubescent children need seek it only three times each day—before the morning prayer, at midday when clothes are put off (al-ẓahīrah), and after the nightfall prayer. These are times of privacy (ʿawrāt), meaning times in which what should be covered may be exposed and entry is naturally embarrassing.

Apparently, “those whom your right hands possess” means male servants, though the masculine expression may include women by generalization (taghlīb), as occurs in hadith. The children intended are those able to distinguish good from bad but not yet pubescent, since they can recognize these private times. Outside them, neither they nor those responsible for them sin by entering without permission, because servants and children must repeatedly come and go in service and requiring permission on every occasion would be burdensome.

The “communications” are divine religious laws, signs pointing to God. God is Knowing and Wise: He knows people’s circumstances and the laws suited to them, and legislates with their welfare and benefit in view.
verses.59: Al-Mizan explains that, once children reach puberty, the concession allowing them to seek permission only three times ends. They must thereafter seek permission as free adult men and women do.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan explains that al-qawāʿid are aged women who have withdrawn from marriage and no longer expect it because, owing to old age, others have no desire to sleep with them. Thus, “who do not hope for a marriage” describes and interprets the term. Some, however, interpret qāʿidah as a woman past menstruation, making the following phrase a restrictive qualification.

The verse is an exception to the general law of hijab: such women may put off their clothes provided they do not display the beauties and ornaments that should be concealed. Majmaʿ al-bayān defines tabarruj as displaying such concealed beauty. Yet restraint—meaning continuing to cover—is better for them. God’s being Hearing and Knowing explains the ruling: He hears what their fiṭrah demands and knows the laws required for their true welfare and benefit.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan apparently understands the verse to permit believers to eat, as needed and without isrāf or ifsād, from the homes of the listed relatives, friends, and persons who have entrusted them with their stores. Although the blind, lame, and sick are expressly named because disability can make earning a living difficult, the addition of “yourselves” shows that the permission is not confined to them but applies equally to all.

The mention of “your houses” may express the unity of believers—so that one’s own house, relatives’ houses, friends’ houses, and houses whose keys one holds are not differentiated—or it may include the houses of one’s son and spouse, as hadith states. “What you possess the stores of” means houses over whose food stores one has charge, such as a custodian, agent, or holder of the keys; “your friend” means a friend’s house. There is no blame in eating either together or separately. The commentary regards this meaning as universal, even if the verse had a particular occasion of revelation, and as most compatible with its context.

The verse then teaches the manner of entering houses: one should greet their inhabitants. Calling this greeting “yourselves” indicates the unity of humanity and, more strongly, of believers; it may also mean mutual greeting, in which entrants greet those present and receive their response. This is a salutation (taḥiyyah) legislated by God, blessed with abundant good and goodly because it brings peace and security to the person greeted. The clarification of these communications is meant to enable people to learn their religion and act by it.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse defines genuine believers: they have true, sincere, certain faith in God’s unity, are confident in their faith, and their hearts are attached to the Messenger. A mark inseparable from this faith is that, when gathered with him for a collective affair (al-amr al-jāmiʿ)—a public matter requiring people to deliberate, consult, and decide, such as battle—they do not leave until they have asked his permission. The verse’s repetition reverses the proposition in order to show that faith and seeking permission are mutually concomitant.

When they seek leave for a personal matter, God leaves the Messenger free to grant permission to whomever he wills or to refuse it. He is also commanded to ask God’s forgiveness for them, thereby comforting them and manifesting divine mercy.
verses.63:
Al-Mizan interprets “the Messenger’s calling (duʿāʾ)” as his summons or command, whether to faith and good works, consultation over an important matter, congregational prayer, or any worldly or otherworldly affair. The ensuing threat against those who steal away confirms this reading and follows the preceding praise of those who remain with the Prophet until given leave: God now condemns those who evade his call, hide behind others, and dismiss his commands.

The commentary therefore rejects two interpretations as incompatible with the following words: that the verse requires people to address the Prophet honorifically rather than as they address one another, or that it warns them not to provoke his imprecation. Those who “steal away” (yatasallalūna) do so cunningly from among the people, taking shelter behind others and concealing themselves (liwādhan); this is turning away from and disregarding the Messenger’s summons.

Fitnah here means an affliction or calamity. In light of this interpretation and the verse’s theme, “his order” more plausibly refers to the Prophet’s call rather than to God’s command, though some take it to refer to God because the prohibition effectively commands answering the Messenger. The warning is that disobeying the Prophet’s order may bring an unwanted trial or painful punishment.
verses.64:
Al-Mizan treats this closing verse as returning to and explaining the opening declaration that the sūrah was revealed and made obligatory (24:1). God’s universal ownership means that everything stands by Him and is known to Him in all its properties, details, and needs. Human beings likewise are known in their true condition and needs; the religion He legislates is among the necessities of their human life, just as the livelihood He provides is necessary for physical survival. His ownership therefore entails His knowledge of the religious laws they need, and He legislates and imposes them accordingly.

The verse also refers to the Day of Resurrection, when people return to Him and He informs them of the reality of their deeds. It thus gives two motives for accepting God’s religion: His laws fulfill needs that He knows, and obedience is required because He will disclose what people have done.
